title: Κύκνος ⟨καὶ δεσπότης⟩
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 174. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Τοὺς κύκνους φασὶ παρὰ τὸν θάνατον ᾄδειν.
sentences.tr: Tous kyknous phasi para ton thanaton āidein.
sentences.l: They say that swans sing at their death.
sentences.n: φασί takes the accusative and infinitive of indirect statement, τοὺς κύκνους … ᾄδειν. παρά with the accusative of time is "right at, alongside" — at the very moment of death.

sentences.t: Καὶ δή τις περιτυχὼν κύκνῳ πωλουμένῳ καὶ ἀκούσας ὅτι εὐμελέστατόν ἐστι ζῷον, ἠγόρασε.
sentences.tr: Kai dē tis peritychōn kyknōi pōloumenōi kai akousas hoti eumelestaton esti zōion, ēgorase.
sentences.l: And so a man, having come upon a swan being sold and having heard that it is a most tuneful creature, bought it.
sentences.i: And so a man came upon a swan for sale, and hearing that it was a most tuneful creature, bought it.
sentences.n: καὶ δή turns from the general report to the one case. Two aorist participles (περιτυχών, ἀκούσας) run ahead of the single finite verb ἠγόρασε — the ordinary engine of these fables. εὐμελής is "of good melody"; the superlative here is less a comparison than a strong "most musical".

sentences.t: Καὶ ἔχων ποτὲ συνδείπνους προσελθὼν παρεκάλει αὐτὸν ᾆσαι ἐν τῷ πότῳ.
sentences.tr: Kai echōn pote syndeipnous proselthōn parekalei auton āisai en tōi potōi.
sentences.l: And once, having guests at dinner, he came up and kept calling on him to sing at the drinking.
sentences.n: παρεκάλει is imperfect: the urging went on and was not obeyed. ὁ πότος is the drinking that follows the meal, the symposium proper, where a performance would be looked for.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ τότε μὲν ἡσυχάζοντος, ὕστερον δέ ποτε, ὡς ἐνόησεν ὅτι ἀποθνῄσκειν ἔμελλεν, ἑαυτὸν θρηνοῦντος, ὁ δεσπότης αὐτοῦ ἀκούσας ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ εἰ σὺ οὐκ ἄλλως ᾄδεις, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποθνῄσκῃς, ἐγὼ μάταιος ἦν, ὃς τότε σε παρεκάλουν, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔθυον. »
sentences.tr: Tou de tote men hēsychazontos, hysteron de pote, hōs enoēsen hoti apothnēiskein emellen, heauton thrēnountos, ho despotēs autou akousas ephē· « All’ ei sy ouk allōs āideis, ean mē apothnēiskēis, egō mataios ēn, hos tote se parekaloun, all’ ouk ethyon. »
sentences.l: But he keeping quiet at that time, and later at some point, when he perceived that he was about to die, lamenting for himself, his master, hearing him, said: « But if you do not sing otherwise, unless you are dying, I was a fool, I who called on you then, but did not kill you. »
sentences.i: But at the time he kept silent, and later, when he perceived that he was about to die, he fell to lamenting for himself; and his master, hearing him, said: « Well, if you will not sing except when you are dying, I was a fool to press you then instead of killing you. »
sentences.n: One long genitive absolute (τοῦ … ἡσυχάζοντος … θρηνοῦντος) holds both of the swan's behaviours, τότε μέν set against ὕστερον δέ, before the main clause arrives. οὐκ ἄλλως … ἐὰν μή is "not otherwise … unless". θύω is properly to sacrifice, but covers killing a beast for the table, and the master means the table.

sentences.t: Οὕτως ἔνιοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἃ μὴ ἑκόντες χαρίσασθαι βούλονται, ταῦτα ἄκοντες ἐπιτελοῦσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtōs enioi tōn anthrōpōn, ha mē hekontes charisasthai boulontai, tauta akontes epitelousin.
sentences.l: Thus some among men, the things they are not willing to grant of their own accord, these they carry out against their will.
sentences.i: Thus some men perform against their will the very things they would not grant of their own accord.
sentences.n: ἑκών and ἄκων are adjectives agreeing with the subject where English uses an adverb, "willing" and "unwilling". The relative clause ἃ … βούλονται is set out in front and then picked up by ταῦτα, a common Greek way of putting the object first.
